candidates.changed_node: the 21-day lookback on the range span (both TS_MIN($low, 21) occurrences and TS_MAX($high, 21)) -> 63
candidates.rationale: Weakness: monotone IC decay, +0.025/+0.027 in 2000-2002 down to +0.0027/+0.0010 in 2012-2013 with stability still 1.00. The magnitude, not the sign, is dying, and the component responsible is the 21-day span: a one-month oscillator is a short-horizon reversal bet, the exact horizon that was competed away after 2003. Widening the span to a quarter makes it a position-in-quarterly-range measure with a longer half-life and lower turnover, and it is the only edit available here: leaving either the numerator or the denominator at 21 keeps a 5- or 9-node subtree identical to the parent, which is itself a live archive member. Windows 5, 21, 126 and 189 are already used for TS_MAX($high, w) / TS_MIN($low, w) in the archive; 63 is free.

Weakness: IC half-life 4.3 days against 0.204 one-way turnover, the worst decay-per-unit-cost pair in the batch. The culprit is TS_SUM($return, 5): a one-week reversal leg that is fully stale inside a week while the $roa leg has a 40-day-plus horizon, so the composite pays weekly rebalancing for a signal it cannot hold. Moving the accumulation to 42 days matches the price leg's horizon to the fundamental leg's, should cut turnover roughly threefold, and separates it from the two archive members that pair RANK($roa) with a 21-day price-position rank. 5-day and 42-day return sums overlap only 12% of their windows, so the parent is not restated.

Weakness: 2003 is -0.0057 and 2009 is +0.0025, the two liquidity-recovery years, while every other year is positive. The regime-sensitive component is the $volume input to the correlation: volume-versus-range comovement is an illiquidity/attention proxy whose sign inverts when market-wide turnover re-rates, which is precisely what happened in 2003 and 2009. Correlating the range against $return instead makes the leg sign-aware (does the wide-range day come with a gain or a loss) rather than flow-aware, so it does not track the turnover regime. One leaf edit; the 15-day window keeps it off the archive's bare 21-day $return-versus-range member.

Weakness: coverage 0.964 is the batch low and |rho| 0.794 is one nudge off the gate, both traceable to the leverage-delta leg, which also gives up 2003 (-0.0069). A 63-day change in $leverage is a balance-sheet risk-appetite proxy: it was rewarded through the 2000-2002 credit contraction and punished in the 2003 rally, and every wrapper around it (CS_RANK, CS_ZSCORE, ABS, MAX, unary minus) is already an archive block, which is what pins rho at 0.794. Swapping the accounting dimension to margin trend keeps the leg's shape and sign convention but changes what it measures; $roa/$roe would not help since they are interchangeable with the prefix. The 42 -> 30 window nudge on the correlation is forced: at 42 that leg is a 7-node subtree identical to the parent's.

Weakness: stability 0.86 and ICIR 0.087 are both the worst in the batch, with 2003 at -0.0117 and 2009 at -0.0001, and the nearest archive member is bare $volume at |rho| 0.714. All three point at the same component: CS_RANK($volume) is a cross-sectional volume level, which is a size and liquidity rank, not a trading signal, so the leg is a static size bet that inverts in large-cap liquidity rallies. Replacing the cross-sectional level with a 63-day within-name ordinal keeps the idea (avoid names being traded unusually heavily right now) while removing the size exposure that causes the two negative years and the 0.714 overlap with the raw $volume member. TS_RANK($volume, w) is used in the archive at 10 and 21 only.

candidates.changed_node: TS_CORR window 63 -> 21 (with the $open normaliser deepened to TS_MEAN($open, 5) to break the shared payload)
candidates.rationale: Weakness: coverage 0.959 is the lowest here and complexity is charged 0.200, both driven by the 63-day correlation window; the same window is why the leg contributes so little that the factor sits at |rho| 0.794 against a near-identical roe-minus-corr member. A 63-day correlation of a range against a turnover series is mostly measuring the shared 3-month trend, not the comovement. Shortening it to 21 puts the leg back in the band where range-versus-volume correlations actually score and restores roughly three percentage points of coverage. The normaliser is shortened to a 5-day average price at the same time because a window-only edit would leave $dollar_volume / ($open + 1e-8) intact as a 5-node subtree of the parent.

Weakness: mean IC 0.00703 is the weakest raw signal in the batch and stability is 0.86, with 2003 at -0.0051 and 2013 at -0.0013. The component responsible is the raw $volume level fed into the correlation: a level with a strong secular drift makes the 21-day correlation largely a measure of whether both series happened to be trending, which is why it flips in quiet trending years. Replacing the level with its 5-day dispersion strips the drift and makes the leg measure whether erratic trading accompanies wide ranges, which is the part of the effect that should be paid. Two-node edit; TS_STD($volume, w) exists in the archive only at 21, and no archive correlation uses a volume-dispersion leg.

Weakness: IC half-life 4.7 days, the shortest in the batch, paired with 0.122 turnover and the lowest mean IC (0.00563). The 5-day difference is the component doing it: a one-week flow shock is stale before the position can earn, so the correlation is fitted to noise that does not persist. Lengthening the difference to a quarter turns the leg into a flow-trend rather than a flow-shock, which is a persistent state and should carry the half-life out past 20 days at lower turnover. One window edit; the archive already holds the 5-day and 21-day versions of this exact correlation, so 63 is the only scale that neither restates them nor sits adjacent to them.

Weakness: 0.417 one-way turnover, four to fourteen times the rest of the batch and charged 0.013 of fitness, against an 8.4-day half-life. TS_RANK($high - $low, 10) is the cause: the daily range is close to white noise day over day, so its 10-day percentile churns every session while the underlying volatility state it is trying to capture moves slowly. Accumulating the range over 10 days before ranking it over 42 measures the same volatility state with a fraction of the rebalancing. TS_RANK($high - $low, 42) is already an archive subtree, so the smoothing is what makes the longer window legal as well as cheaper; TS_SUM($high - $low, w) is used in the archive only at 2, 5 and 21.

Weakness: turnover 0.029 and a 57-day half-life are the best in the batch, so the problem is not cost or horizon; it is |rho| 0.789 against the archive's roe-and-leverage member plus a flat 2003 (-0.0035), 2009 (+0.0009) and 2010 (+0.0024). The component responsible is the TS_MEAN($high - $low, 10) numerator: a 10-day mean range over price is just a slow volatility level, which is the same static risk exposure every other roe-times-range member already carries, and static risk exposures are what go flat in recovery years. Swapping the mean for the 10-day standard deviation of the range makes the leg measure volatility instability rather than volatility level, which is new information at the same cost. The denominator window moves 10 -> 21 because TS_MEAN($open, 10) + 1e-8 is otherwise an intact 5-node subtree of the parent.

prompt:
You are proposing quantitative factor expressions for US large-cap equities.

Universe and data
- S&P 500 point-in-time constituents, roughly 500 names per day.
- Daily bars only, plus point-in-time quarterly fundamentals stamped from the
  report date. Every field is referenced with a leading `$`:
    $open $high $low $close $adj_close $volume $dollar_volume $return
    $roa $roe $operating_margin $leverage $asset_turnover
    $book_per_share $earnings_per_share $accrual_gap
  A bare name such as `close` is not a field and will be rejected.
- Execution convention: the signal is computed after the close of day T and the
  position is entered at the open of T+1.
- The window these factors are fitted and judged on runs from 2000 to 2013.
  Do not reason about anything later; you will never be shown a number from
  outside that window.

Syntax
- Operators are function calls: TS_MEAN, TS_STD, TS_MAX, TS_MIN, TS_RANK,
  TS_DELTA, TS_CORR, TS_COV, TS_SUM, TS_PRODUCT, TS_ARGMAX, TS_ARGMIN,
  TS_DECAY_LINEAR, EMA, DELAY, DELTA, RANK, ZSCORE, CS_RANK, CS_ZSCORE,
  CS_DEMEAN, IF, IF_ELSE, MIN, MAX, ABS, SIGN, LOG, LN, SQRT, POWER, BOUND,
  COUNT.
- Lookback windows must be positive integer literals, e.g. TS_MEAN($close, 21).
- Guard every division with a small epsilon: `/ (TS_STD($close, 21) + 1e-8)`.
- Well-formed example: -RANK(TS_CORR(RANK($close), RANK($volume), 5))

Hard limits every proposal must satisfy, or it is rejected before it is scored
- at most 200 characters
- at most 5 distinct `$fields`
- at most 4 free numeric constants (lookback windows and
  the 1e-8 epsilon guard do not count)
- expression tree depth at most 6
- must not share a complete sub-expression of 4 or more
  nodes with any published Alpha101 formula, or with any factor already in the
  archive. Restating a published alpha is the one thing that is always rejected.
- must cover at least 90% of the panel
- absolute rank correlation below 0.80 against every archive member

Output
- Return valid JSON only, matching the supplied JSON schema. No prose outside it.


TASK: MUTATE. For each parent below, identify its single weakest component and
change ONLY that component.

A mutation is localized: the returned expression must be within
3 tree edits of its parent. Rewriting the idea is not a mutation
and will be rejected. Say which node you changed in `changed_node`, and put the
parent's id in `parent_ids`.

Read the diagnostics: a factor whose IC is positive in most years and negative in two has a regime problem, one with high turnover is paying costs it does not earn back, and one whose IC half-life is short is being asked to predict too far ahead. Change the component responsible for the specific weakness you name.
